'''Tamakushi-hime''' ({{lang|ja|玉櫛媛}}, also written {{lang|ja|玉櫛姫}}) is a woman who appears in [[Japanese mythology]]. She is known as the mother of [[Himetataraisuzu-hime]], consort of [[Emperor Jimmu]] and the first empress. She is also called '''Mishima-mizokui-hime''' ({{lang|ja|三島溝樴姫}}), '''Seyadatara-hime''' ({{lang|ja|勢夜陀多良比売}}) and '''Ikutamayori-hime''' ({{lang|ja|活玉依姫}}).

She is the daughter of {{ill|Mishima-mizokui|ja|三嶋溝抗命|qid=Q135639916}}.

== Records ==
In the passages below, the names in '''bold''' refer to Tamakushi-hime.

=== Age of the Gods and Chigi Hongi ===
The sixth variant account of the eighth section of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' says, introduced with "it is also said", that [[Kotoshironushi]] turned himself into a ''yahiro kuma-wani'' (a great [[Wani (dragon)|wani]]) and visited '''Mishima-mizokui-hime''' (or, as some say, '''Tamakushi-hime'''), and that the child born to them was Himetataraisuzu-hime, empress of [[Emperor Jimmu]].<ref>{{cite wikisource|year=1896|plaintitle=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wspage=61–62|chapter=Book I|publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|author-first=William George|author-last=Aston}}</ref>

According to the "Chigi Hongi" chapter of the ''[[Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'', Tsumi-hayae-kotoshironushi turned himself into a ''yahiro kuma-wani'' and visited '''Ikutamayori-hime''', daughter of Mishima-mizokui, and she bore three children:
* {{ill|Amenohikatakushihikata|ja|天日方奇日方命}} (also called Atatsukushine no Mikoto). He became chief minister in the time of Emperor Jimmu, and is the ancestor of the [[Miwa clan]] and the [[Kamo clan]].
* Himetataraisuzu-hime, empress of Emperor Jimmu and mother of [[Emperor Suizei]] and his brothers.
* [[Isuzuyori-hime]], empress of Emperor Suizei and mother of [[Emperor Annei]].

=== The reigns of Jimmu to Annei, and the Tennō Hongi ===
According to the Jimmu section of the ''Nihon Shoki'', someone (whose name is not given) told the emperor:

: "The child born to Kotoshironushi and '''Tamakushi-hime''', daughter of the god Mishima-mizokuimimi, is named Himetataraisuzu-hime. She is the finest beauty in the land."<ref>{{cite wikisource|year=1896|plaintitle=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wspage=132|chapter=Book III|publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|author-first=William George|author-last=Aston}}</ref>

The Suizei section says Himetataraisuzu-hime was the daughter of Kotoshironushi,<ref>{{cite wikisource|year=1896|plaintitle=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wspage=138|chapter=Book IV|publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|author-first=William George|author-last=Aston}}</ref> and the Annei section says Isuzuyori-hime was also his daughter.

The "Tennō Hongi" chapter of the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' likewise has someone tell Emperor Jimmu:

: "The child born to Kotoshironushi and '''Tamakushi-hime''', daughter of the god Mishima-mizokuimimi, is named Himetataraisuzu-hime. She is the finest beauty in the land."

It also makes Himetataraisuzu-hime and Isuzuyori-hime the daughters of Kotoshironushi.

=== Kojiki ===
According to the Jimmu section of the ''[[Kojiki]]'', when Jimmu was looking for a beautiful woman to make his chief consort, [[Ōkume]] said:

: "Here there is a maiden who is called the child of a god. She is called the child of a god for this reason. The daughter of Mishima-mizokui, named '''Seyadatara-hime''', was very beautiful, and Ōmononushi of Miwa saw her and desired her. When the maiden went to relieve herself, he turned into an arrow painted red, floated down the ditch she was using, and struck her genitals (''hoto''). The maiden was startled and jumped up and ran about. She took the arrow back and laid it beside her bed, and it at once became a handsome young man, who married her, and she bore a child. Her name is Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime no Mikoto, and she is also called Hime-tatara-isukeyori-hime. That is why she is called the child of a god."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=115–117}}</ref>

The child's name was later changed to avoid the word ''hoto'', which became taboo.<ref>{{cite book |author=R. A. B. Ponsonby-Fane |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UVO4AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT412 |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=3 June 2014 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-136-89301-8 |page=412}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Kadoya |first1=Atsushi |title=Ōmononushi |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=126 |accessdate=22 September 2015 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref> For the full story see [[Himetataraisuzu-hime]].

== Worship ==
She is enshrined at [[Shimogamo Shrine]] (Kamo-mioya Shrine), among others.
